about.title: San Marino Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: San Marino's tree-lined residential streets and small commercial stretches along Huntington Drive and California Boulevard mix pedestrian traffic with older sidewalks, private driveways, and retail entrances. When a property is poorly lit, a walkway is cracked, or a spill sits unattended, a quick trip to the store or a walk through a neighbor's yard can turn into a serious fall. California law requires an injured person to show the property owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and failed to fix or warn about it. That means the days and hours right after a fall matter: photos of the exact spot, any visible defect, and a request for surveillance footage before it's deleted. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself, but we can connect San Marino residents hurt on someone else's property with an independent attorney who evaluates these details and works on contingency, so there's no upfront cost to find out where you stand.

whyChoose.title: Why Documentation Matters in a San Marino Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Knew or Should Have Known
items.desc: California requires evidence the hazard existed long enough that a reasonable property owner would have caught it. Photos, maintenance logs, or witness accounts of a prior complaint can help establish this notice element.

items.title: Surveillance Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many San Marino businesses and HOAs overwrite security footage within days or weeks. An attorney can send a preservation letter quickly so that footage of the fall isn't lost before it's ever reviewed.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Eliminate, Recovery
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, even if you're found partly responsible for not noticing a hazard, you can still pursue compensation reduced by your share of fault rather than being barred entirely.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in San Marino?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a premises liability lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity, such as a city building or public sidewalk, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early formal claim. It's worth getting a case reviewed sooner rather than later so this timeline doesn't slip by.

items.question: What should I do right after falling on someone else's property in San Marino?
items.answer: If you're able, take photos of exactly where and why you fell, note the time and weather, and ask if there's a security camera nearby. Report the fall to the property owner or manager in writing and keep a copy. Seeing a doctor promptly also creates a medical record tying your injuries to the incident.

items.question: Do most slip and fall cases in San Marino go to trial?
items.answer: Many premises liability claims resolve through negotiation once liability and injuries are documented, though outcomes vary and nothing can be promised. An independent attorney can review the specific facts of your fall, including any store or sidewalk records, to explain realistic next steps for your situation.
